Command Line.title: Overview
Command Line.content:
Welcome to Linux Lab! In this section you will learn the basics and more of the Linux command line.

The Linux command line can seem intimidating at first, but we at Linux Lab have developed a fun, interactive, and informative way to learn Linux. Reading docs or watching tutorials are also good, but we answer the question "Oh okay thats cool, but when will I ever use this command?".

Well in this section we will go over several commands, understand why its there, and how to use it.

Therefore, the best way to learn is by doing, lets get your journey into the world of Linux started!

Command Line.title: What Is Linux?
Command Line.content:
Linux is a free and open-source operating system based on Unix (an older but groundbreaking operating system from the 1970s). From what started as a hobby project by a college student in 1991 named Linus Torvalds, is now powering most of the digital world.

Here's what is currently running Linux right now:
• The servers behind Netflix, Google, and Amazon
• Your Android phone
• Your car's infotainment system (Tesla, BMW, Toyota, etc.)
• The router connecting you to the internet
• Most smart TVs and IoT devices

In the workplace, Linux skills are essential for:
• Software developers and engineers
• System administrators and DevOps teams
• Cybersecurity professionals
• Hackers
• Data scientists and analysts

The reason Linux is everywhere? It's reliable, secure, customizable, and completely free. While Windows costs hundreds of dollars per license, Linux costs nothing and can be modified for any purpose.

That's why when companies need systems that absolutely cannot fail, like running a bank or launching rockets, they choose Linux.

Command Line.title: Linux Architecture
Command Line.content:
There are 5 main components that make Linux work: Applications, Kernel, Shell, Utilities, and Hardware. As you can see from the image below, these components work with each other to create the Linux operating system. Let's see how they work:



Kernel - The Linux kernel is the core of the operating system and lays down the foundation for how software communicates with hardware. The kernel has 4 main jobs:
  • Memory Management: Keeps track of the device's memory and decides where and how to store content
  • Process Management: Determines which process or program can use the CPU (Central Processing Unit) for a certain time
  • Device Drivers: Acts as a translator between hardware devices (like keyboards, mice, printers) and the software
  • System Calls: Provides a way for programs to request services from the operating system

Shell - This is your command line interface! The shell takes the commands you type and translates them into instructions the kernel can understand. Popular shells include Bash, Zsh, and Fish.

Applications - These are the programs you actually use, like web browsers, text editors, and games. They run on top of the operating system.

Utilities - Built-in command line tools that help you manage your system.

Hardware - The physical components like CPU, RAM, hard drives, and network cards that everything else depends on.

Think of it like a restaurant: Hardware is the kitchen, Kernel is the head chef coordinating everything, Shell is the waiter taking your orders, Utilities are the cooking tools, and Applications are the meals you actually enjoy!

For this section of Linux Lab we will work with the Linux shell and utilities.

Command Line.title: The Command Line
Command Line.content:
example_user@LinuxLab:/$

The Linux command line allows users to input commands to their computers operating system that executes a task via the shell.

In other words, the command line allows you speak to your computer at a powerful level!

This all happens in a text based user interface called the terminal. We at Linux-Lab made you your own personal terminal where the interactive learning will take place. The terminal is placed at your right side (or bottom if you are on mobile) of your screem and it may look like something straight out of a hollywood hacking scene.

As your knowledge and experience with Linux grows, you will begin using your computer in powerful ways. Tasks that take dozens of clicks in a graphical interface can be done with a single command.

For now, we must understand how the filesystem works, because that's where all your files and programs live.

Command Line.title: The Filesystem
Command Line.content:
The core philosophy in Linux is that everything is a file. This means that every file, folder (directory), and even hardware devices are treated as file-like objects to allow for fast and easy navigation throughout your system.

A directory is just the Linux term for a folder. Directories can contain files and sub-directories, which could contain more files and sub-directories, and so on.

This looping technique is called recursion, which is exactly how the filesystem works - like Russian nesting dolls, but for your computer files!

Let's take a look at how it visually works with this example below:



Think of it like a family tree:

  • Root (/): The very top of everything - like the great-great-grandparent
  • Directories: Like family branches - they can have children (more directories or files)
  • Files: The end points - they contain your actual data

Every file and directory has a unique path that tells you exactly where to find it. For example: /home/user/Documents/my_file.txt

This path is like giving someone directions to your house - it starts from the root (/) and follows the directories until it reaches your file.

With that in mind, we can begin introducing commands we have all been waiting for.

Command Line.title: ls

To see what lives in our current directory at any given time, we can use the ls command, which stands for "list"

Command Line.title: cd ..
Command Line.content:
Lets go back to cd and introduce a new technique

Notice how we can go into directories, but how can we go back?

For example, if we are in our Documents/ directory, we should also be able go back to our root directory, or any other directory that lives on top of our curent directory

To accomplish this we need to adjust the syntax and add a argument to the command

An argument is just an additional command that tells the base command what exactly to do. As we get more advanced we will be using arguments to do a lot more cooler stuff!

Let's use the '..' argument to send our directory up a level

cd ..

Note: If you type cd .. into the command line while in your root directory, nothing happens since nothing exists on top of the root directory

Command Line.title: Absolute Path vs Relative Path
Command Line.content:
It would be pretty inefficient if we wanted to navigate around the filesystem if our target source file lived in a far directory. We would probably have to use cd and cd .. a lot to reach our destination. However, this is where absolute and relative paths come into play.
  • An absolute path is the full path to a file or directory from the root directory. It always starts with a forward slash (/) and shows the entire path tree. Example: /home/user/documents/file.txt
  • A relative path refers to a location relative to your current working directory. It does not start with a slash and is shorter to write. Example: ../documents/file.txt

Knowing when to use absolute vs relative paths is key for scripting, navigating efficiently, and writing reliable software.

Command Line.title: cd path/to/source
Command Line.content:
As discussed, navigating around your filesystem in the command line can be done more efficiently by taking the absolute and relative path into account.

For example, lets say we were in our Documents/ dirctory. But we needed to go into our project1/ directory that lives in Projects/. The brute force approach would look something like:

cd ..cd Projects/cd project1/

This approach while isnt technically wrong, is just a slow way to navigate around your filesystem. To fix this, the cd command allows you to put the source path as its argument.

Lets look at the example again, we start in our Documents/ dirctory and have to access Projects/ which lives a level above us right now, so we can use "cd .." to achieve that. We would then be in our root directory which has access to Projects/ which has access to projects1/ which was our target directory.

Adding it all up we get the source path (which also our relative path) as ../Projects/projects1. Lets try this out on the command line!

cd ../Projects/project1

Command Line.title: Searching & Filtering
Command Line.content:
So far we learned how to navigate around our filesystem, along with adding and removing to it. Well now we can begin to tackle the cool and exiting parts of Linux!

Suppose we wanted to look for a file, directory, a word, or any other specific pattern in our filesystem, it would be too long and ineficient to go through every possbile location manually. For example, lets say I wanted to look for a word called "Errors" in a file but the file contains thousands of lines, how can we do this efficiently?

Well the command line allows us to easily solve this problem, one way to solve is with the grep command

Command Line.title: grep
Command Line.content:
The grep command allows us to search and filter specific patterns in files

grep -options "pattern" file

-The options flag is an optional command that is used for an additional level of filtering, somne of these flags include:

- -i: Case insensitive search

- -v: Invert match (show lines that don't match)

- -r: Search recursively through directories

- -n: Show line numbers

- The pattern is the text or regular expression you want to search for, which is usually under quatation marks

- The file argument simply specifies which file(s) to search in

Command Line.title: grep "pattern" file
Command Line.content:
The grep command is one of the more exciting commands to use since it will basically automate a task. Lets take a look at using the grep command at its most basic form

Traverse to our Documents/ directory and find how many times "And" appears in Shakespeare.txt, which contains Shakespeare's "Sonnet 18" poem, try it out!

grep "And" Shakespeare.txt

Command Line.title: grep -n "pattern" file
Command Line.content:
As mentioned before, the grep command can take in optional flags. One of these optional flags is '-n'.

The -n flag will output the number line(s) the pattern was in, lets take a look at this with an example.

In the same Documents/ directory lets observe how many times "British" appears in Declaration.txt, which contains the United States Declaration of Independece

grep -n "British" Declaration.txt

Command Line.title: grep -c "pattern" file
Command Line.content:
Continuing on with grep, another common flag that is used is '-c', which is used to return the total count of appearences a pattern matches too.

To test this, in the same Documents directory, lets retrieve the total count where "moon" appears in John F Kennedy's "We choose to go to the moon" speech under Kennedy.txt

grep -c "moon" Kennedy.txt

Command Line.title: wildcard*
Command Line.content:
By now we can see how useful the grep command is, but what if we needed to search our entire directory for a pattern in all of our .txt files? We could individually look at every file with grep, but what if we had hundreds of files to look at?

Well this special syntax called the "wildcard" character represented in the command line by a star '*' allows us to do just that.

The wildcard character works by grabbing everything that satisfies its pattern. So instead of looking through every file that ends in .txt, we can call the wildcard character on those .txt files represented syntatically as '*.txt'

The wildcard character is a very powerful tool that you should keep in your Linux arsenal. Lets run through a quick example in our Documents/ directory to see it in action.

grep "all" *.txt

The command here will look for all instances of "All" in every file that ends in .txt in our Documents/ directory

Command Line.title: find
Command Line.content:
We have gone over how to search for patterns with grep and how useful that can be, but what about looking for specific files or directrories in your filesystem?

Well the find command is a powerful tool for searching through your file system that helps you locate the actual files themselves based on certain criteria like the size of the file, permissions, and more.

The find command takes in 3 arguments:

  • 1st argument: the source path to your desired file or directory you are looking for. Remember, the source path is the relative path since find will start at your current directory.
  • 2nd argument: an optional flag that is just an additional filter that helps specify what we are looking for like an exact name, size, permission, and more.
  • 3rd argument: simply the exact filename or directory name you are looking for.

Lets take a look at how the find command looks syntactically:

find /path/to/source -options -filename

Command Line.title: sort
Command Line.content:
The sort command is one of the more powerful commands in Linux, it allows us to sort content of a file and see the output based on the parameters we give it. By default sort arranges lines alphabetically in ascending order. Which means that if numbers are in the file, sort will treat the numbers as strings and only sort by the first digit of a number.
sort -flag filenameLike with other commands, the flag here is optional so lets just first look at a simple example.

In our Documents/ directory, lets take a look of our grocery list. Then, we will use this simple sort command and observe what happens, try it out! sort grocery_list.txt

Command Line.title: sort -flag
Command Line.content:
We can now mess around by adding flags to the sort command to add an additional layer of filtering. Here are a few major ones:
  • -r: Reverses the order of the sort output.
  • -n: Sorts numbers numerically instead of alphabetically (so 2 comes before 10).
  • -u: Removes duplicate lines so only unique results are shown.
Go ahead and try out the reverse flag in grocery_list.txtsort -r grocery_list.txt

Command Line.title: The Output Redirection Operators: '>', '>>'
Command Line.content:
Excitingley, Linux allows you to redirect output to an existing file or even a new file on the fly!

Suppose we are outputting content to the terminal, but what if we we wanted that contnent to go inside a file instead? Well there are 2 operators that allow us to do that.

The '>' operator overwrites existing content to a file, so the old content that lived in that file will now only contain the new content./p>

The '>>' operator appends to a file, so it will add on to the existing content instead of overwriting it.

There are several Linux commands that support these redirection operators like: grep, ls, echo, find, cat, and more.

Overwrite content: [command] > [file]

Append to contnent: [command] >> [file]

Lets start with a basic example using echo to demonstrate more clearly.

Command Line.title: The Overwrite Operator: '>'
Command Line.content:
Lets enter our Documents directory and overwrite Shakespeare.txt with new content we will provide as an argument

echo "I Love Linux!" > Shakespeare.txt

This command will completely erase the existing content and replace it with the argument "I Love Linux!". Try it out!

Command Line.title: The Appending Operator: '>>'
Command Line.content:
In the same Shakespeare.txt file lets now add to the file with the '>>' operator by writing "Dinosaur!" to the file. Try it out!

echo "Dinosaur!" >> Shakespeare.txt

Notice how instead of overwriting the contenet like how the '>' operator does, it just adds to it!

Coming up soon, we will look at examples of how to redirect the output of grep, ls, cat, etc.. but it is generally the same syntax and principle

Command Line.title: Permissions In Linux
Command Line.content:
In Linux every file has permissions that allows or prevents users to read, write, and execute a file or program. We can desrcibe these terms on the terminal as:

r – Read (can view the file or list the folder)

w – Write (can modify the file or folder)

x – Execute (can run the file if it’s a program or enter the folder)

Also, there are permissions for 3 type of users:

Owner – the person who owns the file

Group – a group of users assigned to the file

Others – everyone else

Command Line.title: ls -l
Command Line.content:
Permissions can seem confusing at first, but we will clear it up. To see the output of your file permisions we can use the ls -l command, lets walk through the output!

-rw-r--r-- user group 2025-02-27 01:24:04 648 Shakespeare.txt

To start off, there are 10 dashes, but the very first dash will determine if it's a file or directory. The next 9 are grouped into 3, which is important to understand to make modifications. The first group of 3 gives you the permissions for the owner (or the user if you own it) of the file, the next 3 give you permissions for the group (a collection of users like a devs team that are working on this), and the last 3 represent the others (a collection of users who are not the owner and not apart of the team). Lets look at the output one by one.

  • -As mentioned earlier, the first - indicates it's a regular file. If it were a directory, it would show d.
  • rw- The owner can read and write the file.
  • r-- The group can only read the file.
  • r-- Others (everyone else) can also only read the file.
  • user The name of the file's owner.
  • group The group assigned to the file.
  • 2025-02-27 01:24:04 The last modified date and time.
  • 648 The file size in bytes.
  • Shakespeare.txt: The name of the file.

In summary, this file is readable by everyone, writable only by the owner, and not executable by anyone.

Command Line.title: Alphabetic Mode
Command Line.content:
The Linux permisions can be expressed in 2 ways, one being the Alphabetic mode which we have been working with already but lets take a closer look.

Up to now, we know that in order to see the permissions of a file, directory, or program we have to read the permissions for that owener's, group's, or other's dashes, but the placement of the dashes do matter. For example, lets look at this image for a quick quick example. As mentioned earlier a few times, the vert first dash is not relevant to the permissions, it just simply tells us if its a file or directory.

Therefore, we split the next 9 dashes into the 3 groups as mentioned before. The first dash always represents the read permissions. If the permission has the r, we know permissions are valid. However, if was a dash that means it does not have read permissions. In fact the dash for the owner's, group's, and other's mean the same thing, that this body does not have this permission.

The second dash represnts the write permission, which states if this body is able to write to this file. If there is a w then writing permisions are valid. Otherwise, it would be invalid and represented with the dash.

Liekwise, the last permission for a body represents the execution permission. Meaning if this body is allowed to run this program or file. If they are allowed then it will be represented with x, otherwise it's not allowed and will be represented with a dash

Command Line.title: Octal Mode
Command Line.content:
The 2nd way we can represent Linux permissions is through a numeric or octal mode. The octal mode allows us to simplify permissions by using numbers instead of letters!

Each permission type has a numeric value:
  • r (read) = 4
  • w (write) = 2
  • x (execute) = 1
We add these numbers together to form a single digit for each group: owner, group, and others.

For example:
  • rwx = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7
  • rw- = 4 + 2 + 0 = 6
  • r-- = 4 + 0 + 0 = 4

When written in octal mode, permissions are represented as three digits, one for each body. For instance:
  • 777 = rwx for owner, rwx for group, rwx for others
  • 644 = rw- for owner, r-- for group, r-- for others
  • 755 = rwx for owner, r-x for group, r-x for others
Overall, this makes octal mode the more efficient and cleaner approach to set permissions in Linux, especially when setting permissions with the chmod command.

Command Line.title: chmod
Command Line.content:
Now that we have some level of understanding of how permissions work in Linux, suppose we didn't have access to read, write, or execute a file, how could we solve this?

The chmod (change mode) command allows us to modify file permissions. The basic syntax is:

chmod [options] mode file

As discussed earlier, there are two ways to specify permissions:

Alphabetic Mode:

  • u: user/owner
  • g: group
  • o: others
  • a: all (equivalent to ugo)
  • +: add permission
  • -: remove permission
  • =: set exact permission
  • r: read permission
  • w: write permission
  • x: execute permission

Examples:

  • chmod u+x script.sh - Add execute permission for the owner
  • chmod go-w file.txt - Remove write permission for group and others
  • chmod a=r document.pdf - Set read-only permission for everyone

Octal Mode:
  • 4: read permission
  • 2: write permission
  • 1: execute permission

We add these numbers for each category (owner, group, others):

  • chmod 755 script.sh - Owner: rwx (7), Group: r-x (5), Others: r-x (5)
  • chmod 644 file.txt - Owner: rw- (6), Group: r-- (4), Others: r-- (4)
  • chmod 600 private.key - Owner: rw- (6), Group: --- (0), Others: --- (0)

Common permission patterns:

  • 755: Standard for executable files (rwxr-xr-x)
  • 644: Standard for data files (rw-r--r--)
  • 700: Private executable files (rwx------)
  • 600: Private data files (rw-------)

However, if you need to change permissions for files you don't own, you'll need to use the sudo command to override the existing permission

Command Line.title: sudo
Command Line.content:
The sudo command is one of the more important commands in Linux as it allows you to execute commands with the security privileges of another user, typically known as the superuser (root).

This gives you temporary administrative access to perform tasks that regular users cannot do.

The name 'sudo' stands for 'superuser do' or 'substitute user do'. When you run a command with sudo, the system will typically ask for your password to verify your identity.

Basic syntax:

sudo command_to_run

Common examples:

Modifying File Permissions: sudo chmod [options] file_name>

- Installing software: sudo apt install package_name

- Editing system files: sudo nano /etc/hosts

- Restarting the system: sudo reboot

Always use sudo with caution, as it gives you the power to modify critical system files and settings that could potentially damage your system if used incorrectly.

Command Line.title: chmod: change user permissions
Command Line.content:
Let's take it slower and break down how to use sudo with chmod, traverse to the root directory and enter the Work/ directory.

Use ls -l to see the permissions on these files, try using cat on 'daily_logs.txt' to see whats inside the content.

Notice how we dont have read permissions for 'daily_logs.txt' so we cannot cat the content to view it since we don't have the permissions for it!

Also, notice how we dont have authorization to modifiy the file since we are not the user.

There are a few ways to tackle this problem, but lets use sudo for now. Since we are adding reading permissions and we don't own the file ourselves we must syntatically use: sudo chmod u+r daily_logs.txt

Which just means "Hey Linux, treat me as the root user, so please add reading permissions to this user!

Try it out!

Command Line.title: chmod: change group permissions
Command Line.content:
Let's explore how to change group permissions for files.

In the same Work/ directory that we were just in, run ls -l to see the current files again

Take a look at 'sales_report.txt' - notice how the group doesn't have write permissions for this file, so members of the group can read it but can't make changes!

Let's fix this by adding group write permissions. Similar to how we modified user permissions, we'll use chmod but with the 'g' option instead of 'u' to target the group permissions.sudo chmod g+w sales_report.txtTry it and then use ls -l again to see how the permissions have changed!

Command Line.title: chown
Command Line.content:
The chown command changes the owner and group of files and directories in Linux systems. It is another solution to change your file permissions wihout using sudo, since the owner will now be you. However if you don't own the file at first, you will need to use sudo to allow the chown command to take use. After this, you would no longer need sudo

Basic syntax: chown [newowner] filename

Common examples:

  • chown alice file.txt - Changes owner to alice
  • chown bob:devlopers project.py - Changes owner to bob and group to developers
  • chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/ - Recursively changes ownership for all files in a directory

Overall, while sudo provides temporary elevated privileges, chown makes permanent ownership changes that remain after your session ends. This is especially useful for:

  • Setting proper ownership for service accounts (like web servers)
  • Delegating file management without giving sudo access
  • Enabling collaboration in multi-user environments
  • Following security best practices

Since changing ownership often requires elevated privileges, you'll typically use it with sudo: sudo chown [newuser] /path/to/source

Command Line.title: chown: change owner of a file
Command Line.content:
In the Work/ directory, lets take a look how chown can be used and how it affects your system.

Run ls -l and you will notice that the owner for daily_logs.txt isn't you (user). Which means you wouldn't be allowed to alter the state of the system without constanly using sudo.

The permanment solution to this is to use chown with sudo to change ownership back to you. Lets see how it works by running this command

sudo chown user daily_logs.txt

Note: In this enviroment the owner for a file that you own is under user

If you have made it this far consider yourself a Linux command line guru. By now we have covered most of the core Linux commands that you will need, but there are still some convienient commands that would be beneficial so lets quickly go over them.

Ever wondered how many lines, words, or characters a file has? Well of course Linux has a command that makes it super easy to do just that with the command wc (word count).

wc [option] [file]As you can see the wc command can take in a optional flag argument. But for now lets just take a look at a simple example.

By default, if you give wc no flag arguments it will display the number of lines, number of words, and the number of characters of the desired file(s). Traverse to the Documents/ directory to see some magic happen.

Command Line.title: Piping |
Command Line.content:
"Do one thing and do it well, and work together through pipes."

This is the most advanced command and technique we will touch, but sadly it wont work in our simulated envrioment. However, it is so important that we have to mention it. So what are pipes?

Pipes let you chain commands together, taking the output of one command and feeding it as input to the next. Think of it like a factory assembly line where each station does one specific job, then passes the work to the next station.

The pipe symbol `|` is responsible for connecting the commands together: command1 | command2 | command3

Example #1 - Count files in a directory

ls | wc -l This command will find all the files in the directory and return back the count

Example #2 - Unique sorted lines of a file

cat file.txt | sort | uniq This command will display the sorted content in file.txt and remove duplicates keeping it unique.

Example #3 - Find .log files containing "error" and sorting the results

find ./ -name "*.log" | grep "error" | sort In our current directory, this would find all the log files, look for all instances of error, and sort the results.

Piping can get pretty complex but can deal some really powerful results. I strongly suggest opening up your own terminal on your machine and practicing. The best way to understand pipes is to play with them!

Networking.title: Networking
Networking.content:
In Computer Science, Networking refers to the connection of computers communicating to each other to produce emails, streaming, websites, gaming, messages, and the rest of the internet services we all enjoy today!

Learning all the nuances of how Networking actually works like the OSI Model, protocols, routers, switching - requires a dedicated course to obtain the knowledge and certification.

However for this networking section, we will just introduce the basic networking theory. And apply it to the command line to use powerful networking Linux commands.

Networking.title: Local Ip Address, Local Address Network (LAN)
Networking.content:
Every device on the internet has an address that is used to identify where that device lives. For example, your house has an address that allows shipments, friends, or family to locate your house that returns a shortest path.

Well your computer, smartphone, television, and other devices carry their own address called an IP address (which is short for a Internet Protocol address) and their role allows a device to communicate through the internet. However, your IP address will differ whether you are on a Local Area Network (LAN) or a Wide Area Network (WAN). For now, we will just look at your LAN IP address, which is just 4 sets of digits like:192.168.1.1

Simply put, a Local Area Network is the local grouping of connected computers that are responsible for fetching and sending out data. Some LAN's use wires like an ethernet cable for speed (typically seen in a office or home setting), and others use a wireless method using radiowaves like WIFI (typically seen in a cafe, school, or building setting). You are most likely on a LAN right now!

Networking.title: IPV4 vs IPV6
Networking.content:
Since 1983, the internet used the standard 32 bit integer (we will discuss this later) IP address to identify devices on the internet. 192.1.0.255You probably have seen this already in your life since it's still used today, however as technology advanced and more people began using the internet, we faced a big problem. We ran out of IP addresses!

How did we combat this? Well simple, we just made the IP address bigger!

On June 12, 2012, IPV6 (Internet Protocal Version 6) was officialy launched worldwide.2001:db8::ff00:42:832Instead of the original 32 bit address IPV4 used, IPV6 uses an outstanding 128 bits! But how much bigger is that? Let's find out in the next lesson.

Networking.title: How does an IP address work?
Networking.content:
We have talked about how IP address use 32 bits or 128 bits, but what exactly does that mean?

Bits are just 1's and 0's, and is the way how computers communicate and process information, also known as binary.

In binary, we read from right to left and every digit goes by a power of 2. The first digit starting on the right is: 2¹ which is 2, then the next will be 2² which is 4, followed by 2³ which 8 and so on.

For ip addreses, they range between 0-255 and are seperated by the period('.') which is known as an octet. Each octet will hold 8 bits, and the bits (if you do the math) will return back the decimal value of that octet. Since there are 4 octets and each octet contains 8 bits, that means the entire address contains 32 bits! Hence why IPV4 is a 32 bit address! Let's take a look at a IPV4 address as an example. From the example, we can see how it works, the octets are split into their binary value which will all add up back to the human readable decimal value.

As mentioned earlier, IPV4 ran its course since it only provided 4,294,967,296 (232) possible unqie addresses. At the time this was seen as enough but the internet and technology exploded, which gave rise to IPV6.

For IPV6, its ip address uses a slightly more complex system but its roughly the same idea. Since its a 128 bits, that means it provides 2(132) is a number so big its enough to fill every star in the universe with 5.4 quadrillion grains of sand, so I think we are safe for now.

Networking.title: Classes
Networking.content:
Right now would be a good time to mention that your ip address isn't just a random set of numbers between 0-255, they are a reflection of what kinda Network you are in!

Back in the early days of the internet, engineers created a system called Network Classes to organize IP addresses based on network size. Think of it like organizing neighborhoods - some are small residential streets, others are massive cities!

There are three main classes you'll encounter:

Class A Networks (1.0.0.0 - 126.255.255.255)
These are the massive networks. If your IP starts with a number between 1-126, you're on a huge network that can support around 16 million devices. These are typically used by large corporations or internet service providers.
Example: 10.5.100.50

Class B Networks (128.0.0.0 - 191.255.255.255)
The medium-sized networks. If your IP starts with 128-191, you're on a network that can handle about 65,000 devices. Perfect for universities or medium-sized companies.
Example: 172.16.10.25

Class C Networks (192.0.0.0 - 223.255.255.255)
The small networks! If your IP starts with 192-223, you're on a small network with about 254 devices max. This is what you'll see at home, small offices, or cafes.
Example: 192.168.1.100 (Looks familiar, right?)

Here's the cool part: just by looking at the first number of any IP address, you can instantly tell what size network you're dealing with!

But here's the problem that led to subnetting - what if you need something in between? What if 254 devices is too small, but 65,000 is way too big? That's where subnetting comes to the rescue, which we'll explore next!

Networking.title: Subnets
Networking.content:
We have discussed that network classes give us three fixed sizes: huge (Class A), medium (Class B), or small (Class C). But what happens when none of these sizes fit what you actually need? Well we kinda figured it through subnetting.

Subnetting refers to the network process of taking one big network and chopping it up into smaller, more manageable pieces.

Think of subnetting like this: imagine you own a large apartment building (your original network). Instead of having one massive space where everyone lives together, you divide it into separate floors or apartments. Each apartment becomes its own subnet(a smaller network within the bigger one).

Why would you want to do this?

Organization: You can separate different groups. Put the accounting department on one subnet, engineering on another. Just like putting different departments on different floors of a building!

Security: You can control who talks to whom. Maybe the guest WiFi subnet can't access the company servers subnet.

Performance: Smaller networks mean less traffic congestion. Instead of 1000 devices all shouting at once, you have groups of 50 devices in organized subnets.

Efficiency: No more wasting IP addresses! Instead of giving a small company an entire Class B network (65,000 addresses) when they only need 500, you can create custom-sized subnets.

Here's a simple example: Let's say you have the network 192.168.1.0 (normally 254 devices). With subnetting, you could split this into:

  • 192.168.1.0 - Subnet for employees (126 devices)
  • 192.168.1.128 - Subnet for guests (126 devices)

Same building, but now it's organized into two separate apartments!

The magic happens with something called a subnet mask, which tells your computer: "Hey, these IP addresses are in your neighborhood, but those other ones are in a different subnet."

Networking.title: Subnet Masks
Networking.content:
Alright, so we know subnetting lets us divide big networks into smaller ones. But how does your computer actually know where one subnet ends and another begins? That's where the subnet mask comes in

Remember when we looked at the ifconfig command and saw that cryptic? netmask 255.255.255.0Well, that's your subnet mask in action!

Think of a subnet mask like a postal system. When you write an address, you have a street address (like "123 Main Street") and a city (like "Springfield"). The subnet mask tells your computer: "Here's the city part (network), and here's the street address part (host)."

Let's break down the most common subnet mask: 255.255.255.0

In binary this looks like:
11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000

Here's the rule: wherever you see 255 (or 11111111 in binary), that part represents the network portion. Wherever you see 0 (or 00000000 in binary), that's the host portion.

So for an IP address like 192.168.1.100 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0:

  • Network part: 192.168.1 (this is like your "city")
  • Host part: 100 (this is like your "street address")

This means any device with an IP starting with 192.168.1.___ is in the same subnet, meaning they're all in the same "city" and can talk to each other directly!

But a device with an IP like: 192.168.2.50 That's in a different "city" (different subnet), so it will need defualt gateway or router to communicate.

You'll also see subnet masks written in CIDR notation like /24. This just means "the first 24 bits are the network portion." Since 255.255.255.0 has 24 ones in binary, it's the same as /24.

Next time you run ifconfig, you'll know exactly what that netmask is telling you about your network neighborhood!

Networking.title: Default Gateway
Networking.content:
We found out that when we try to access a service outside of our network, we need the default gateway to route us out of local network and find the outside network we want to speak to.

Think of your default gateway like the front door of your apartment building. When you want to visit someone who lives in your building (same subnet), you can walk directly to their door. But when you want to visit someone in a different building (different network), you have to go through the front door and out into the street!

Your default gateway is typically your router, and it does the job. That little box sitting in your home or office that connects your local network to the internet. It usually has an IP address like 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1

Here's how it works:

Let's say your computer (192.168.1.100) wants to visit Google (142.250.72.206). Your computer first checks: "Is Google in my subnet?"

Using the subnet mask 255.255.255.0, your computer realizes:

  • My network: 192.168.1.x
  • Google's network: 142.250.72.x
  • These don't match - Google is NOT in my neighborhood!

So your computer says: "I need to go through the front door!" and sends the request to the default gateway (192.168.1.1). The gateway then says: "No problem, I'll find the path to Google for you!" and routes your request out to the internet.

On the command line we can see this process taking place with the Linux command:ip route

Networking.title: ip route
Networking.content:
The ip route command shows your computer’s routing table. It decides where to send network traffic, describes how the default gateway works, and which network interfaces are used to reach different IP ranges.

In other words, think of ip route as your Google Maps directions (the planned route).

Lets try it on the terminal by running this command: ip route Breakdown: 

default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlp3s0 proto dhcp src 192.168.1.217 metric 600
192.168.1.0/24 dev wlp3s0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.217 metric 600
  • default via 192.168.1.1: This is the default route — if no other route matches, traffic goes to your router (192.168.1.1).
  • dev wlp3s0: Indicates the wireless network interface being used.
  • proto dhcp: This route was configured by DHCP (A network service whos job it is to automatically assign every device network settings on its network)1.
  • src 192.168.1.217: The system’s IP address on that interface.
  • metric 600: A priority value — lower values are preferred.
  • 192.168.1.0/24: A route for all devices on your local network (192.168.1.x), which are reachable directly without needing a gateway.

Networking.title: Servers, Clients, and Hosts
Networking.content:
When we interact with a network, devices typically fall into two main roles: Servers and Clients.
  • Server – A server is a computer or device that is specifically designed to receive requests and respond with the appropriate data (like web pages, streaming movies, sports, and so on). For example, when you log into a website, your device (the client) sends a request to the server. The server's job is to process the request by checking your login info—and respond with the correct data, such as your profile page, payment info, and more.
  • Client – A client is the device or program that initiates the request. Most commonly, it's your computer, phone, or browser accessing a service like a website or email.
  • Host – A host refers to any device connected to a network that can send or receive data. Both clients and servers are considered hosts.

Networking.title: Networking Connections
Networking.content:
When we are online gaming, surfing the web, streaming movies, or watching live TV, we will occasionally come across network performance issues, often referred to as "lag" or, in technical terms, network latency.

Network latency issues can be caused by hardware performance, physical distance, packet loss, or network congestion (too much traffic on a network).

To test the speed or how "strong" a connection is to a server or computer, we can use the ping command followed by a destination argument. The argument can either be the ip address or the full website domain you're trying to connect to, as seen below:

ping 192.168.1.1ping some_website.com

Networking.title: ping
Networking.content:
On the command line lets ping google to see how strong our connection is to their server:

ping 142.250.72.206Or more cleanly: ping google.com

The output at first glance (like many Linux network commands that you have probably come across alrady) can be cryptic and intimidating, but we'll break it down and see the important information it gives us.

  • 64 bytes from nuq04s45-in-x0e.1e100.net – This shows the domain name of the responding server. It confirms that we successfully reached a Google server.
  • icmp_seq=1 – This is the sequence number of the ping packet, starting at 1 and increasing with each request (we will learn more about this later).
  • ttl=114 – TTL stands for 'Time To Live', which tells how many more hops (routers) the packet can go through before being discarded. It also gives a rough idea of how far away the server is.
  • time=23.4 ms – This is the round-trip time in milliseconds. Lower values mean faster responses and better connection quality.

Networking.title: DNS - Domain Name System
Networking.content:
Whenever we search for a website in a browser, we type in something simple like google.com or amazon.com. But how does your device actually know where to go?

This is where the Domain Name System (DNS) comes in. It's a protocol that translates those easy-to-remember domain names into IP addresses (the real location of a website on the internet).

Think of DNS like a phonebook for the internet. When you type in a domain, your system reaches out to a DNS server, which looks up the name and responds with the matching IP address. Once your system has that, it can connect to the correct server and load the site.

Without DNS, we'd have to memorize strings of numbers like 142.250.190.78 instead of just typing 'google.com'. Take a look at a visual walkthrough below!

Networking.title: nsloopkup
Networking.content:
Through the Linux command line we can interact with a DNS server with nslookup which stands for 'name server lookup'.

The command will return the IP address of some_website.com and the DNS server used for the query. Try it out on the command line with this example:

nslookup google.comBreakdown:
Server: 192.168.1.1
Address: 192.168.1.1#53
Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   google.com
Address: 142.250.72.238
  • Server: The DNS server your system is using to resolve the domain.ndx
  • Address: The IP address of that DNS server with port 53 (used for DNS communication).
  • Non-authoritative answer: Indicates the response is from a cached or forwarded DNS server, not directly from the authoritative source.
  • Name: The domain name you queried (google.com).
  • Address: The resolved IP address of the domain.

Note: Sometimes, multiple IPs may be shown depending on the DNS setup of the domain.

Networking.title: Ports
Networking.content:
When we use a radio and want to find a rock music station, we tune to a specific frequency — like 104.7 MHz. That frequency tells the radio which station to listen to. Once the connection is made, we receive the output resulting in rock music.

The internet works in a similar way. Because the internet handles many types of traffic (web browsing, email, file sharing, streaming, etc.), it uses ports to organize that traffic. Each port represents a specific type of service.

For example:

  • Port 80 – HTTP (websites using plain text)
  • Port 443 – HTTPS (secure websites)
  • Port 25 – SMTP (sending email)
  • Port 53 – DNS (resolving domain names)

When your computer connects to a website, it doesn’t just connect to an IP address — it also connects to a port on that address. This way, the server knows what kind of service you’re asking for.

Port numbers range from 0 to 65535, but most common services use ports below 1024, known as well-known ports.

Networking.title: Protocols
Networking.content:
Suppose you are at a party and you meet someone new, the instinct for both parties is to shake each other's hands and greet. This process could be seen as a protocol, meaning that both parties engaged in societal rules and guidelines to greet each other. The internet works the same way.

In networking, a protocol is a set of rules and standards that govern how devices communicate with each other over a network. Just like social protocols help people interact smoothly, network protocols ensure that different computers, servers, and devices can understand each other and exchange information reliably.

Why Do We Need Protocols?

Imagine trying to have a conversation where one person speaks English, another speaks French, and a third speaks Japanese - without any common language or translation rules, communication would be impossible. Network protocols solve this problem by establishing:

  • Common Language: How data should be formatted and structured
  • Timing Rules: When to send data and when to wait
  • Error Handling: What to do when something goes wrong
  • Connection Management: How to start and end communications

How Protocols Work

Think of protocols as layers of rules, like a formal dinner party:

  1. Physical Layer: Like having proper seating arrangements - how the actual connection is made
  2. Data Layer: Like using the right utensils - how information is packaged
  3. Application Layer: Like following conversation etiquette - how programs interact

Networking.title: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocal
Networking.content:
We have all seen it before, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the protocol across the web. It works by underlying rules and guidelines that operate over other fundamental protocols like TCP and UDP.

What is HTTP?

HTTP is the foundation of data communication on the World Wide Web. Every time you click a link, submit a form, or load a webpage, your browser is using HTTP to communicate with web servers. Think of it as the postal system of the internet, it defines how messages are formatted and transmitted between your browser (the client) and websites (the servers).

HTTP's Protocol Stack

HTTP doesn't work alone, it relies on lower-level protocols to actually transport data:

  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Provides reliable, ordered delivery of HTTP messages
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Sometimes used for faster, but less reliable communication
  • IP (Internet Protocol): Handles routing messages across the internet

HTTP sits on top of these protocols, focusing on the structure and meaning of web communication while letting TCP/UDP handle the actual data transmission.

How HTTP Works

HTTP follows a simple request-response model:

  1. Request: Your browser sends a request to a web server asking for a specific resource (like a webpage, image, or video)
  2. Response: The server processes the request and sends back the requested resource along with a status code
  3. Display: Your browser receives the response and displays the content to you

HTTP Status Codes

When a server responds, it includes a status code to indicate what happened:

  • 200 OK: Everything worked perfectly
  • 404 Not Found: The requested page doesn't exist
  • 500 Internal Server Error: Something went wrong on the server
  • 301 Moved Permanently: The page has moved to a new location

So we can conclude that sockets are the foundation to create a connection, but how will data flow across the connection? Well this is where TCP & UDP come into play.

Networking.title: Sockets
Networking.content:
This is where Networking gets serious, especially if you are interested in network programming.

A socket is the 2-way endpoint between a client and server. Meaning that before any data is sent over the internet, a 2-way connection must be established. So, how does it work?

Think of a socket as a telephone connection between two parties. Just like you need to dial a number and wait for the other person to pick up before you can have a conversation, computers need to establish a socket connection before they can exchange data.

A socket combines:

  • IP Address: The "phone number" that identifies the specific computer
  • Port Number: The specific "extension" or service on that computer.
  • Protocol: The "language" they'll use to communicate.

Socket Connnection Steps

  1. Server Setup: The server creates a socket and "listens" on a specific port (like waiting by the phone)
  2. Client Request: The client creates a socket and attempts to connect to the server's IP address and port
  3. Connection Established: If successful, both sides now have a direct communication channel
  4. Data Exchange: Information flows back and forth through this established connection
  5. Connection Closed: Either side can terminate the connection when finished

Networking.title: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
Networking.content:
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is one of the more popular techniques used to transfer data across a socket (the internet). It works by establishing a reliable, connection-oriented communication channel between two devices.

What Makes TCP Special?

Think of TCP like a registered mail service - it guarantees that your package (data) will arrive at its destination in the correct order and in perfect condition. If something goes wrong during delivery, TCP will detect the problem and resend the data automatically.

Key Features of TCP

  • Reliable Delivery: TCP ensures that all data sent actually reaches its destination
  • Ordered Data: Messages arrive in the exact same order they were sent
  • Error Detection: TCP can detect corrupted or missing data
  • Flow Control: It prevents overwhelming the receiving device with too much data at once
  • Connection-Oriented: A connection must be established before any data transfer begins

The Three-Way Handshake

Before any data can be sent, TCP establishes a connection through a process called the three-way handshake:

  1. SYN: Client says "I want to connect"
  2. SYN-ACK: Server responds "OK, I'm ready to connect"
  3. ACK: Client confirms "Great, let's start communicating"

This is like two people agreeing to have a phone conversation before they start talking.

How TCP Ensures Reliability

TCP uses several mechanisms to guarantee reliable data transfer:

  • Sequence Numbers: Each piece of data gets a number so the receiver knows the correct order
  • Acknowledgments: The receiver confirms when data arrives successfully
  • Retransmission: If data doesn't arrive or gets corrupted, TCP automatically resends it
  • Checksums: Built-in error detection to catch corrupted data

When is TCP Used?

TCP is perfect for applications where accuracy is more important than speed:

  • Web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS)
  • Email transmission
  • File transfers
  • Online banking
  • Any application where losing data would be a problem

Networking.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol
Networking.content:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a fast and lightweight technique used to transfer data across a socket (the internet). It works by sending data quickly without establishing a formal connection or guaranteeing delivery.

What Makes UDP Different?

Think of UDP like dropping postcards in a mailbox - you send them quickly and hope they arrive, but you don't get confirmation of delivery. UDP prioritizes speed over reliability, making it perfect for situations where losing a little data isn't catastrophic.

Key Features of UDP

  • Fast Delivery: No connection setup means data can be sent immediately
  • Connectionless: No need to establish a connection before sending data
  • Lightweight: Minimal overhead means more bandwidth for actual data
  • No Guarantees: Data might arrive out of order, duplicated, or not at all
  • Simple: Fewer features mean less complexity and faster processing

How UDP Works

UDP's approach is straightforward:

  1. Package Data: Wrap the data in a UDP header with basic information
  2. Send Immediately: Fire the data packet toward its destination
  3. Move On: Don't wait for confirmation - just keep sending more data

There's no handshake, no acknowledgments, and no retransmission if something goes wrong.

UDP vs TCP: The Trade-off

While TCP is like a careful conversation with confirmations, UDP is like shouting across a crowded room:

  • Speed: UDP is much faster because it skips reliability checks
  • Efficiency: Less overhead means more actual data gets transmitted
  • Risk: Some data packets might get lost or arrive in the wrong order

When is UDP Used?

UDP is perfect for applications where speed matters more than perfect accuracy:

  • Online gaming (a few missed frames won't ruin the experience)
  • Video streaming (better to skip a corrupted frame than pause the video)
  • Voice calls (brief audio dropouts are preferable to delays)
  • DNS lookups (quick queries that can be easily repeated if needed)
  • Live broadcasts (real-time data where delays would be worse than minor losses)

Networking.title: traceroute
Networking.content:
The traceroute command allows us to see actual path the data packets take to reach a destination across a network. It shows each hop (router) the packet passes through, along with the time it takes to reach each one. This is useful for diagnosing network delays or identifying where a connection might be failing.
The syntax for traceroute is: traceroute example_website.com Lets try out an example on the terminal: traceroute google.com Breakdown of the output: 
  • Hop Number: The number at the start of each line (e.g. 1, 2, 3) shows the hop count.
  • IP Address: The IP of the router or device at that hop (e.g. 192.168.1.1).
  • Time: The time (in milliseconds) it took for the packet to reach that hop. Multiple times show retries.
  • *: A star means no response was received from that hop (could be blocked or timed out).
This helps you spot slow or failing routes in a network.

Networking.title: telnet
Networking.content:
The telnet command is a tcp client based command that allows us to manually connect to a remote host on a specific port. In other words, the command allows us to check if a service (like a web server, SSH server, or mail server) is running and reachcable on that port.

Syntax: telnet [example.com] [port] Let's try a basic example by testing if we can reach google and listen on port 80. telnet google.com 80

Breakdown:

  • Trying 2607:f8b0:4005:810::200e... - This shows the IP address telnet is trying to reach (IPv6 or IPv4).
  • Connected to google.com. — Success! A TCP connection to port 80 is established.

If the connection is successful, you're now manually connected to Google’s web server over TCP. At this point, you could type an HTTP request (we will discuss later), or simply close the connection. Overall, this is useful for quickly testing if a port is open and listening.

Networking.title: netstat/ss
Networking.content:
The Linux command line allows you to inspect active ports and sockets using socket statistics tools.

You can use the older netstat command, but the modern and faster alternative is ss.

Try out the command in the command line and we will breakdown the output
ss -tuln
This command shows all TCP, UDP, and ports that are currently listening, in numeric format.

Output Breakdown:

  • Netid: The protocol being used (e.g. tcp, udp)
  • State: Connection state (e.g. LISTEN, ESTABLISHED)
  • Recv-Q: Bytes received and queued
  • Send-Q: Bytes waiting to be sent
  • Local Address:Port: Your IP address and port
  • Peer Address:Port: The remote IP address and port (if connected)

Using ss helps you check which services are currently listening on your machine, making it easier to identify running servers or background processes. It’s also a valuable tool for auditing open ports to ensure no unnecessary services are exposed, which is important for system security. Additionally, ss allows you to debug port binding and network issues by showing exactly which IPs and ports are in use, helping you pinpoint configuration problems quickly.

Networking.title: HTTP vs HTTPS
Networking.content:
We have gone over HTTP already, but what is its counterpart HTTPS?

What is HTTPS?

HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is essentially HTTP with a security layer added on top. Think of HTTP as sending a postcard through the mail - anyone handling it can read your message. HTTPS is like sealing that same message in an encrypted envelope that only the intended recipient can open.

Encryption

The main difference between HTTP and HTTPS is that HTTPS encrypts all data traveling between your browser and the web server. This means:

  • HTTP: Data travels in plain text that anyone can intercept and read
  • HTTPS: Data is scrambled using encryption, making it unreadable to eavesdroppers

How HTTPS Works

HTTPS uses SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security) to create a secure connection:

  1. Handshake: Your browser and the server agree on encryption methods
  2. Certificate Exchange: The server proves its identity with a digital certificate
  3. Key Exchange: Both sides create a shared secret key for encryption
  4. Secure Communication: All data is encrypted using the shared key

Visual Indicators

You can easily identify HTTPS websites:

  • Lock Icon: Appears in your browser's address bar
  • Green Address Bar: Some browsers show enhanced visual security indicators
  • URL Prefix: Starts with "https://" instead of "http://"
  • Port Number: Uses port 443 instead of port 80

Why HTTPS Matters

  • Eavesdropping: Prevents others from reading your data
  • Man-in-the-Middle Attacks: Ensures you're communicating with the real website
  • Data Tampering: Detects if information has been modified during transmission

Essential for:

  • Online banking and financial transactions
  • Shopping and credit card information
  • Login credentials and passwords
  • Personal information and private communications

The Cost of Security

HTTPS does have some trade-offs:

  • Slightly Slower: Encryption/decryption takes processing power
  • More Complex: Requires SSL certificates and proper configuration
  • Additional Overhead: Extra data in each request for security headers

However, modern computers and networks make these costs minimal, which is why most websites now use HTTPS by default.

Networking.title: GET vs POST
Networking.content:
While we surface around a website, we interact with the browser's HTTP methods, which are requests from a client to a server. These requests come in different forms, but the most commom requests are GET and POST methods.

  • GET - A GET request is a type of http request that retrieves web pages, displays local session information like a username, and 3rd party data in the form API's (will discuss more about API's later). For example, whenever you click on a web page that displays content, you are sending a get request to the server that responds back with your desired content. To achieve fast lookups for web content, GET requests enter the URL and are visible so your browser can cache the content (a computers way to temporarily remembering). For instance, you are currently working on the 'Networking' section module on our Linux Lab website. If you look at the URL you will see something like: https://linux-lab.live/src/pages/lesson_page/lesson.html?module=NetworkingThis displays the source path of where the code lives in the server, but at the tail end you will see 'module=Networking' which is the GET request you send to the server that flips between different modules, resulting in the content you currently see right now.
  • POST - A POST request is another type of http request that is responsible for adding data to the server in a secure manner. The most common POST request is when you enter a credit or debit card to make a transactional purchase, or when you enter your email, username, and password to sign up/ log in on a web application.

Networking.title: curl
Networking.content:
The most powerful network Linux command that is used to extract web content, modify web content, and even hack, is the curl command.

The curl command works by transferring data to or from a server and operates on top of HTTP methods like GET, POST, and even interact with API's.

Using the curl command can get complicated since it can do many things and takes in a lot of parameters, but here is the basic syntax: curl [options] [URL..] Like with other Linux commands we have come across, [options] is an optional argument that does filtering and modifications, we will use it later on.

For now, let's take a look at a basic example, we will use the curl command to extract the HTML code (the code websites use to structure their websites) from Oracle and output it in the terminal. Try iy out! curl https://www.oracle.com

Networking.title: curl - Headers
Networking.content:
Before we enter a webpage and view all the content, your browser sends chunks of information that will be needed for the user. This information will include the following:
  • User-Agent – Identifies the browser, version, and operating system being used.
  • Accept – Tells the server what content types (like HTML, JSON, XML) the client can understand.
  • Host – Specifies the domain name of the server the client wants to connect to.
  • Connection – Indicates whether the client wants to keep the connection open or close it after the response.
  • expires - The expiration date and time when the browser will consider this version of the web page 'old' and will fetch a new copy
  • cache-control - The permission details that decides if the content can only be cached to your browser (private), or can be cached to 3rd parties to enhance the performance time for everyone using the website (public).
    • Let's run through a headers example using the curl command with an option command.

    curl -I https://www.google.com We added the '-I' flag here which stands for 'HEAD Request' which tells curl to not extract the full HTML content, but rather just the headers. Try it out!

Networking.title: API's - Application Programming Interface
Networking.content:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules and protocols that allows different software applications to communicate and interact with each other. APIs define the methods and data formats that applications use to request and exchange information, enabling developers to build complex features by integrating with other systems or services. They act as a bridge between different software components, simplifying development and promoting modularity.

One of the most popular types of APIs is the REST API, which follows the REST (Representational State Transfer) architectural style designed specifically for web services. REST APIs use standard HTTP methods and are known for being simple, scalable, and stateless.

Key characteristics of REST APIs include:
  • Use of standard HTTP methods: Such as GET to retrieve data, POST to create new data, PUT to update existing data, and DELETE to remove data.
  • Statelessness: Each request from client to server must contain all the information needed to understand and process it, with no client context stored on the server between requests.
  • Resource-Based: Resources (like users, products, or orders) are identified using URLs (Uniform Resource Locators).
  • Multiple Data Formats: While JSON is the most commonly used format, REST APIs can also send and receive XML, HTML, or plain text.
  • Scalability and Simplicity: The design of REST APIs supports easy scaling of applications and straightforward implementation.

Overall, APIs, and especially REST APIs, play a crucial role in modern software development by enabling seamless integration between different applications and services over the web.

Networking.title: WAN (Wide Area Network)
Networking.content:
Earlier, we discussed that a LAN (Local Area Network) is the local network where devices like your phone, laptop, or printer communicate. For example, in a home, café, or office, we learned how to find your local IP using the `ifconfig'. But what about your public IP address?

This is the IP that the outside world sees when you connect to the internet.

When your device sends a request to the internet, it goes through your router. Your router has a WAN (Wide Area Network) IP address, which is typically the same as your public IP. This IP is assigned by your ISP (Internet Service Provider) and allows your router, and by extension, your entire local network to communicate with servers on the internet across a large geographical area.
